extracted.intended_audience: aspiring comedy writers; writers of topical satire and humorous essays
extracted.subtask_short: writing topical satire and humorous essays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting topical satire and comedic essays that balance specificity, social commentary, voice development, and inventive formats; aimed at writers developing voice and producing timely humor tied to pop culture. Includes practical tips on premise selection, perspective, and publishing trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodical analysis of structure and humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down the writing process to figure out how pieces are structured, what makes something funny, and what resources are available to learn more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carlos describes using his engineering background to analyze structure and identify resources for improvement. Treat writing analytically to learn patterns and craft, but recognize limits (see 'avoid formulas').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on formula; evolve your comedic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy formulas stop working after a while; you must constantly evolve and find new ways to be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He warns that, unlike engineering, formulas eventually fail (example: 'nobody is doing Three Stooges-style slapstick nowadays'). Innovation and adaptation are necessary to stay fresh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specificity to make jokes land
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific details make a story unique and help the humor land harder, even when addressing universal experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in the Hocus Pocus essay, details like 'Second Empire Victorian built in 1870' or 'Italianate-style cupola' signal a fancy old house and sharpen jokes about repairs. Specificity often improves comedic effect rather than diluting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick source material familiar enough to reach readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor pieces to movies/topics most people will at least have heard of so there's something for everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarity with the movie helps readers understand the premise and context; choosing recognizably popular films broadens potential audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write from the perspective of minor or imagined characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Step into the mindset of minor characters or imagined characters to examine their point of view within the world of a movie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique opens new comic possibilities by shifting focus away from well-trodden main characters and exploring overlooked angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place characters in plausible but unexplored situations to subvert expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Create scenarios that are believable for a character but haven't been explored in the original story to generate fresh humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: imagining Superman receiving a denied visa — a bureaucratic, plausible situation that casts a known character in an unexpected, comedic light while preserving core traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain core character traits while inventing new narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: When subverting expectations, keep characters' core traits intact so the new situation rings true and generates humor from contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greaves emphasizes plausibility for characters — their reactions should make sense even in satirical premises, which strengthens the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose premises that articulate audience feelings on real issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Tap into how people feel about a story or real-world event and pick a premise that helps articulate those feelings through satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: paralleling Jurassic Park's hubris with political decisions during Covid created resonance because it echoed public sentiment. The premise should help express an emotional truth, not just be clever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distance social commentary through fictional frames
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fictional universes (movies, etc.) to discuss serious topics indirectly so commentary can be made in a sillier, less direct way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing about 'horrible things' in a fictional setting reduces directness and lets you keep the piece silly while still making a point; other distancing techniques are also acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust readers; avoid over-explaining the point
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't tell the audience the point directly; trust them to understand implications and keep the piece playful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greaves advises keeping things as silly as possible and relying on the reader to infer commentary rather than spelling it out, which preserves comedic momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop voice through practice, deadlines, and quick turnarounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Find mediums (webseries, timely satire) that force deadlines and produce a high volume of work to hone your voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greaves attributes voice development to producing lots of pieces under constraints; quick turnaround formats provide intrinsic motivation and practice. He notes persistence through many rejections before getting a breakthrough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experimental formats to take creative risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ unconventional formats (e.g., patent applications, declassified memos) to create fresh comedic structures and experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such formats can be riskier but offer original ways to present satire. Greaves used experimental essay formats in his self-published book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-publishing trade-offs: creative control versus promotion burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-publishing gives ultimate creative freedom to take risks and experiment, but shifts the burden of promoting the book onto the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greaves valued creative control (enabling experimental formats) but found marketing and self-promotion uncomfortable and time-consuming; working with an editor/illustrator helped refine direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research source material to find silly or tieable plot points
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewatch and study source films to spot plot points that feel silly or can be connected to modern society as satirical premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greaves rewatched classics to identify moments to riff on (example: Dead Poets Society textbook-ripping scene) and built essays by playing up contrasts like wealth disparity between schools.
